item.title: Trump sons' investments have won billions in Pentagon contracts since his election
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
President Donald Trump announced a $6.6 billion investment with AI defense company Anduril Industries on Tuesday -- the most recent government funding agreement into a company with investment ties to the president's sons. The Trump administration announced the Navy will support $2.9 billion of the total cost to help create a new facility in Baltimore County, Maryland, that will manufacture critical parts for the Virginia-class nuclear-powered fast-attack submarine. "In a tremendous victory for our country and for the city of Baltimore, Anduril is investing $3.7 billion in a state-of-the-art shipyard that will be known forever as Arsenal-2," Trump said at an event announcing the investment. Damien Eagers/PA Wire IRISH Press Association via AP Images - PHOTO: Donald Trump visit to Ireland "Right here in Sparrows Point, you'll build the next generation of American submarines, including autonomous subs, torpedo tubes, and critical components for our cutting edge Virginia-class attack submarines," Trump said. Republican senator calls for Judiciary Committee to subpoena Donald Trump Jr. and Hunter Biden 1789 Capital -- a venture capital firm that lists Donald Trump Jr. as one of six partners along with three founders -- claimed a major stake in Anduril in June 2025 from a $2.5 billion investment into the company. Since that investment, Anduril has been awarded 135 other contracts with the U.S. government and to date has received around $1.8 billion from those agreements, according to active defense contracts posted to SAM.gov , the official system for government contracting. Anduril did not respond for comment on its contracts or investments from 1789 Capital, though the company has been awarded contracts dating back to 2019, according to USASpending.gov The company is one of the largest manufacturers to receive an investment from Donald Trump Jr. and his brother Eric Trump, but they are not the only one. Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP Photo - PHOTO: President Donald Trump speaks at an event for Anduril Industries, Inc., at Sparrows Point Shipyard, Oct. 6, 2026, in Sparrows Point, Md. An ABC News analysis found defense companies backed by the president's sons, including Anduril, have now raked in more than $6 billion dollars in active or promised government contracts since those investments were made, according to the government's official contract reporting. This comes as Congressional Oversight Democrats continue to demand the Pentagon's inspector general investigate the approved deals. "Refusal to investigate these serious allegations will raise significant concerns about whether your office is able to perform its statutory duty as an independent watchdog over DoD," Sens. Richard Blumenthal, Elizabeth Warren, Robert Garcia and Tammy Duckworth wrote in a letter to Platte B. Moring, III, the Pentagon's inspector general, in May. President Donald Trump announces creation of 'Super Intelligence Force' AI task force Peter Morrison/AP Photo - PHOTO: Trump Ireland A spokesperson for the Trump brothers denied any wrongdoing. "Don and Eric are experienced business leaders who have built and invested in businesses across a wide range of industries for decades, long before their father first ran for public office. Their investment decisions are based solely on their independent business judgment and personal convictions and they do not seek to influence, direct, or participate in any government decision, procurement, award, regulatory action, or other governmental process. Attempts to portray their ordinary investment activities as improper are a deliberate distortion of the facts," the spokesperson said. The White House declined to comment. Drone investments Shortly after Trump won the presidency, Donald Trump Jr. was named an adviser for Florida-based drone manufacturer Unusual Machines -- a company which had not previously won any government contracts. In October 2025, Unusual Machines scored a direct U.S. Dept. of Defense agreement for 3,500 orders of National Defense Authorization Act-compliant motors, with a potential order of 20,000 on the way in 2026. The Trump brothers are also listed as "notable investors" for the U.S. drone company Powerus, the company announced in March 2026. Despite not having any government contracts previously, Powerurs won its first Air Force purchase order just one month later for an undisclosed amount. In July, Powerus was awarded up to $90 million for aerial-denial unmanned aircraft systems from the U.S. Air Force. ABC News asked Powerus if it was concerned at all about the involvement of the Trump brothers in the company, given its active contracts. "Defense procurement is merit-based. You can't sell the government something that won't protect a soldier, and nobody in the procurement chain risks their career routing a contract to a company whose equipment doesn't work," a spokesperson for Powerus said. "Neither Donald Trump Jr. nor Eric Trump is an advisor to Powerus, and neither is involved in the company's day-to-day business," the spokesperson continued. "Their interest is indirect, held through American Ventures, an investor in the company." Manufacturing investments Trump-linked investments extend into the manufacturing industry, with the brothers combining for more than $1 billion across companies in mining, quantum computing and aerospace. Oversight Democrats in their letter to the DoD criticized Donald Trump Jr.'s portfolio in raw materials, citing an August 2025 investment into Vulcan Elements, a rare-earth mining company harvesting critical materials for defense manufacturing. That same month, the Office of Strategic Capital loaned Vulcan Elements $620 million to expand its operation. Alex Brandon/AP Photo - PHOTO: Election 2026 Republicans Vulcan Elements did not respond for comment when asked about these contracts and the investments from 1789 Capital. The firm also invested $60 million in Texas-based Firehawk Aerospace, according to firm portfolios provided by PitchBook. In the same month, Firehawk won a $4.9 million Air Force contract to "Advance Hybrid Rocket Engine Development," according to a company press release. Firehawk would later secure tens of millions more -- $3.2 million in May 2026 , an undisclosed "multimillion-dollar" contract with the Air Force Research Laboratory in July and $24 million in Dept. of Defense munitions contracts in August, according to company press releases and active contracts. Firehawk Aerospace has been awarded government contracts across both the Biden and Trump administrations since the company's founding in 2019. In a statement to ABC News, Firehawk said its award is "solely the product of engineering expertise and capacity." Our focus is the duty in front of us, making the arsenal of the U.S. and our allies stronger," a Firehawk spokesperson said. PsiQuantum also signed a $100 million letter of intent with the Department of Commerce and another $125 million with the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency in May and July of 2026. PsiQuantum did not respond when asked for comment on these investments. Anthony Behar/Sipa USA via AP - PHOTO: NJ: President Trump At 2026 LIV Golf New York - Round Four Automation investments Trump-linked investments were found in the automation sector. Eric Trump touted a $24 million contract in April -- the company's first -- according to Eric Trump and CEO Sankaet Pathal's statements on Fox News. ABC News found a $391 million 1789 Capital investment into Hadrian -- a highly automated, AI-driven manufacturing company -- in the early days of 2026. Hadrian did not respond for comment when asked about these contracts. Congressional Democrats continue to sound the alarm over these investments, referring ABC News to their May demand to the Department of Defense to launch an investigation into the president's family. "We hope that your office will take seriously these latest concerns about corruption in the DoD award process and fulfill your statutory responsibility by initiating a review," the senators wrote in their letter. item.title: Woman's killing reignites Okinawa anger over U.S. military presence
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
TOKYO - Mounting anger over a U.S. Marine arrested on suspicion of killing a Japanese woman in Okinawa has once again inflamed long-simmering tensions over the U.S. military presence in the prefecture, as Tokyo seeks to enact the most sweeping change in its security strategy in Okinawa in decades. Lance Cpl. Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, was taken into custody on suspicion of killing Anna Yagi, 39, who died of suffocation in a hotel Saturday, local police said. Ballard is also suspected of stealing Yagi's wallet and other belongings. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. Ballard has denied the allegations, police said. The case was referred to the local prosecutor's office, though it remains unclear whether authorities will prosecute Ballard. Under a long-standing agreement governing U.S. troops in Japan, Ballard is subject to Japanese jurisdiction because the alleged crime occurred while he was off-duty. The incident drew immediate backlash from Okinawan and national authorities. Both the U.S. ambassador to Japan and the commander of U.S. Forces Japan were summoned to Tokyo, and Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi called the case "extremely brutal and heinous" in a statement on X. About 180 people held a protest outside the U.S. Embassy in Tokyo on Tuesday evening, and a demonstration outside the Foreign Ministry is scheduled for Thursday evening. U.S. Forces Japan said Tuesday that all personnel stationed in Okinawa would suspend all activities for 48 hours starting Wednesday and undergo training on standards and discipline. Troops will also be subject to a curfew for a 30-day "Period of Reflection." The incident comes amid efforts by both governments to grapple with what the Japanese Foreign Ministry has described as "the most severe and complex security environment since the end of World War II," with Japan at the center of a campaign to reinforce the U.S.-led security order amid threats in the region from China, North Korea and Russia. Takaichi, a China hawk, last year suggested that Japan could become involved in defending Taiwan, a self-governing island claimed by China, in case of Chinese invasion, breaking with decades of policy. As the prefecture closest to Taiwan, Okinawa is central to Takaichi's "southwest shift" strategy of bolstering the Japanese military presence in the region. Okinawa already bears a disproportionate burden in hosting American forces in Japan. The prefecture contains about 70 percent of U.S. military facilities in the country, despite representing less than 1 percent of Japan's land area. Local residents have long voiced anger and resentment over crime, environmental pollution and overcrowding resulting from military bases in the region. For over a decade, the political reality in Okinawa has been characterized by the central government in Tokyo backing - and local governors rejecting - plans for strengthening both the American and Japanese military presence in the region. But the newly inaugurated governor of Okinawa, Genta Koja, ran on a more conciliatory platform, dropping his predecessor's opposition to the construction of a new U.S. Marine Corps base in Henoko and expressing willingness to work with Tokyo on the southwest shift. Saturday's arrest is likely to complicate the governor's approach. Koja said in his first policy speech Tuesday that he would make "protecting Okinawa" a major pillar of his administration and that he would call for a reduction in U.S. military bases in Okinawa in a meeting with Takaichi on Wednesday. Koja now faces a "very important question," said Fumiaki Nozoe, a professor of international politics at Okinawa International University. "When Japan's national security policy comes into conflict with the lives and livelihoods of Okinawa residents, which side will he stand on?" In the past, crimes committed by U.S. forces in Okinawa have pushed the Pentagon to offer concessions to the local government. After three U.S. servicemen raped a 12-year-old Okinawan girl in 1995, public outrage spurred Washington to announce plans to shutter Marine Corps Air Station Futenma, though the base remains open. Saturday's incident is unlikely to result in concessions given the ongoing push to militarize further in Okinawa, Nozoe said. "I would imagine that the Japanese and U.S. governments are essentially thinking that they can manage the damage, let the issue gradually fade away, and then proceed with the next Japan-U.S. joint exercises and the plans for the realignment of U.S. forces," he said. "But if they do not take some kind of fundamental measures, another incident or accident will occur, and there will again be a backlash in Okinawan society." Yang reported from Taipei, Taiwan. item.title: Bessent says inflation and bond yields will drop after the Iran war. Others aren't so sure.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent says the economy is "accelerating" and inflation, along with bond yields, will come back down once the conflict in Iran ends. "Right now, we have this energy shock that's generated by the Iran conflict, and headline inflation is about 3.5%. But my message is underlying inflation — core inflation — is down to about 2.3%," Bessent said at the Pennsylvania Chamber of Commerce on Monday night. He asserted that median wage growth is in line with headline inflation, and that "we will get to the other side of this Iran conflict. Energy will come back down, and the wage growth will continue." Read more: How oil price shocks ripple through your wallet, from gas to groceries He said 1 million private sector jobs have been created this year, while government jobs have been trimmed by 300,000. "Real wage growth comes from private sector jobs, and I think we're just starting to see the acceleration here," he said. But not everyone sees the wage picture the same. Gregory Daco, chief economist for EY, notes that average hourly earnings rose at an annualized pace of 3% in September , marking the slowest pace of the post-pandemic cycle. He said he expects inflation in September, as measured by the Consumer Price Index, to clock in at 3.6%, and as a result, he anticipates that wages adjusted for inflation will likely fall 0.6% year over year, marking a sixth consecutive month of contraction. "While strong wealth effects from stock market gains continue to support solid aggregate consumer spending, the growing income squeeze affecting households is likely to cap spending growth heading into 2027," Daco said. Joe Brusuelas, chief economist for RSM, agrees that the economy accelerated into the third quarter, but he asserts that inflation is not easing, pressuring wages and purchasing power. Brusuelas maintains that the CPI report due out next week will show that wage growth adjusted for inflation has been flat to negative since the start of the Iran war. "It's far more likely that declining real wages begin to act as a mild drag on growth heading into the final quarter of 2026 and early 2027," he said. Higher bonds: strong economy or oil prices? Bessent also addressed the spike in long-term Treasury yields, saying he believes the run-up is a function of headline inflation and higher energy prices stemming from the war. Once the conflict ends, he said, longer-term bond yields will come down to levels seen in mid-February before the war. "I don't know if this conflict's going to end next week, next month, in two months, but I believe on the other side of this, energy prices will be much lower and interest rates, mortgage rates will come back down," he said. Read more: When will mortgage rates go down again? While Bessent thinks much of the increase in bond yields can be chalked up to higher energy prices, top Federal Reserve policymakers view the strength of the economy as a main driver. Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh noted at a recent press conference that economic strength is the primary driver of long-term yields. Cleveland Federal Reserve president Beth Hammack said recently that she thinks a number of factors are driving up yields, including a strong economy. "I think that the growth numbers have come in in a pretty solid way," she said. "I think that expectations of continued performance, if you look at earnings and profits for various public companies, they've been coming in above expectations, and there have been signs of resilience that I think the markets are starting to price in." Philadelphia Federal Reserve president Anna Paulson also said recently that she sees a resilient economy that's showing some signs of increased momentum despite tariffs and higher oil prices. She noted that consumer spending has been strong, the AI build-out is driving investment, and the labor market is stable. Meanwhile, Fed Vice Chair Philip Jefferson sees the economy as likely to show continued resilience, despite higher prices, and he anticipates investments in AI will continue to support growth this year. He said he expects near-term real GDP growth to remain roughly the same as in the first half of the year. The upshot? If bond yields have risen in large part because of stronger growth, then the war ending and oil prices falling may mean yields drop somewhat, but still remain high. item.title: Some Republicans fear $1 billion may not be enough to overcome midterm challenges
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
WASHINGTON (AP) — Republicans are entering the final month of the midterm campaign increasingly anxious that the $1 billion at their disposal may not be enough to fend off sweeping losses as the party reckons with President Donald Trump's unpopularity, persistent cost concerns and the fallout from the war in Iran . The cash advantage, spread out across a half-dozen groups, is driven largely by the Trump-aligned MAGA Inc., which had nearly $416 million in cash on hand at the end of August and began stepping up its spending on critical races in September. But that money may have come too late, forcing the president's group to pay much higher rates because of the shrinking availability of air time. Four Republican Senate campaign officials said groups that reserved advertising time last spring paid much lower rates than MAGA Inc. and its affiliated groups. Instead, by waiting until September, Trump-connected organizations are sometimes paying more than five times what they would have spent if they acted earlier. A representative of MAGA Inc. familiar with the group's strategy said its spending has allowed Republicans to keep races more competitive than they would have been otherwise. In some cases, the group has been the only one on the air criticizing Democratic candidates. The MAGA Inc. representative and the Republican Senate campaign officials spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss internal strategy. The challenge is acute in places like Texas, where Trump will travel on Wednesday for the second time in a week to stump for Republican Ken Paxton's Senate campaign. The state hasn't elected a Democratic senator since 1988, yet MAGA Inc. has spent more than $22 million in the past month, according to the ad tracking firm AdImpact. Another group, Texas PAC, which is aligned with Senate Majority Leader John Thune , has spent more than $83 million on advertising in the past month, an extraordinary amount to protect what's normally a safe Republican seat. One of those advertisements, which featured Paxton's estranged wife saying she's supporting the full Republican ticket, aired across the United States last weekend during a football game between the Dallas Cowboys and the Houston Texans. Candidates are charged a lower advertising rate than outside groups, so the late infusion of super PAC cash has come at a steep price. MAGA Inc., which is running ads primarily on streaming services, has been charged roughly $894 per airing, according to AdImpact, while Texas PAC has been charged roughly $809 for a mix of broadcast and streaming. That compares with about $290 for Democratic nominee James Talarico's campaign, also on broadcast and streaming. Those averages mask some of the more glaring disparities. For example, during a football game last month, Texas PAC was charged $450,000 to air a single spot in the Austin market. Talarico's campaign paid $50,000 for a spot during the same game in the same market, according to AdImpact. Elections are a referendum on the power of money The 2026 campaign is shaping up as a referendum on the power of money in American politics. Democrats freely acknowledge their disadvantage, relying instead on anti-Trump sentiment among voters and targeted messaging on issues like corruption. Some Republicans, meanwhile, are open about the challenge of trying to spend their way out of a tough campaign at this late stage. Neil Newhouse, a longtime Republican pollster, echoed concerns that his party was deploying its cash too late. “After the votes are counted, I think we're going to find the most effective advertising in terms of communicating message and moving voters and poll numbers, the most effective time was advertising that happened well before Labor Day, not after it,” he said. “A million dollars of advertising in October is a drop in the bucket." Thune's group began pulling back in North Carolina last week, a sign of the party's challenge in the Senate race there. The state's outgoing Sen. Thom Tillis has been increasingly vocal about his party's vulnerabilities and recently said that, even with a strong cash advantage, “in the last month, you pretty much have to place your bets.” “If we have endless resources, then we should spend endlessly in every state,” he said. “Absent endless resources, you've got to make data-driven decisions about where you can win.” The midterms mark the first national election since the Supreme Court in June erased limits on how much political parties can spend in coordination with candidates for Congress and president, injecting even more money into a political system already awash in cash. Money alone doesn't translate into victory There's plenty of evidence that money alone doesn't translate into victory. Democrat Kamala Harris entered the final stretch of the 2024 campaign with significantly more money than Trump but went on to lose every critical swing state and the White House. Elon Musk's $25 million didn't lift his preferred candidate to a Wisconsin Supreme Court seat last year. And Tom Steyer didn't advance to the general election in the California governor's race despite pumping $216 million of his own money into the campaign. The $1 billion that Republicans have amassed compares with roughly $579 million held by a comparable collection of major Democratic groups. Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer said his party is facing an “obscene” amount of spending that could swamp them in the midterms. “We're never going to have as much money as them,” he said in an interview. “I sum up the election in this sentence: Can a massive Republican advantage in money beat a massive Democratic advantage in better candidates and political climate? item.title: Christa Pike's condition 'bodes well for a good recovery.' What happens to her next?
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Christa Pike is conscious and speaking in the hospital after surviving Tennessee's attempt to execute her last week , an outcome her legal team described as "unprecedented," and one that has raised questions about what happens next in her case. Pike, 50, was sentenced to death in 1996 for the murder of her classmate, Colleen Slemmer, and spent 30 years on death row. Her execution was scheduled for Wednesday, Sept. 30, but two doses of the lethal injection drug pentobarbital failed to kill her. She was taken to the hospital, where she received lifesaving care. Pike's survival has brought intense scrutiny to Tennessee's execution procedures. Gov. Bill Lee suspended the one remaining execution scheduled for this year, and the state's top prison official, Correction Commissioner Frank Strada, is stepping down at the end of October. Pike's lawyers said the resignation was "justified, but it does nothing to help Christa now. What happened to her Wednesday reflects a systemic failure that goes far beyond any one person," they said in a statement issued Sunday, according to ABC News . Slemmer's mother, May Martinez , described the situation as a "mess" and said she was left without justice. What is Christa Pike's condition? When Pike arrived at the hospital, her arms were "swollen, burned and blistered," her lawyers wrote in a legal filing Friday. Her lawyers believe the IV lines were placed incorrectly or her veins burst, so that some or all of the drug went into the tissue of her arms instead of her bloodstream. "Against all odds, Christa Pike is conscious, speaking, and continues to receive critical medical care," her legal team wrote in a statement issued Tuesday. "Her recovery is medically unprecedented. Her prognosis remains unclear but, at a minimum, we expect a long recovery." Dr. Joel Zivot, a medical expert who has consulted with Pike's legal team, told the Associated Press that the latest update "bodes well for a good recovery," but said that the full picture of her long-term health will not be clear for some time. "She has recovered to a certain degree that she's able to be off a ventilator and able to speak, but in no way would I announce her free of further serious risk," he said. "There's still a lot of bad things that can happen here." Pike, pictured in 2007, is conscious and speaking in the hospital, according to her legal team. via REUTERS / REUTERS Deborah Denno, a criminologist and professor at Fordham Law School, told the BBC that she was "absolutely astonished" that Pike was conscious and speaking. "They did everything they were supposed to do as part of the execution process, and it simply didn't work," she said. "This has never happened before." Dr. Zivot told the BBC that her survival was "unusual," adding, "Most people who get lethal injection die from it. In fact, pretty well everyone, except Christa." Seattle University Law Professor Michael Russo told the Associated Press, "There's nobody else in the history of the death penalty in this country who has gone through what she's been through." The incident with Pike comes a handful of months after the botched attempt to execute Tony Carruthers . In May, Tennessee stopped the execution of Carruthers after staff placed an IV into his right arm, but were unable to insert a secondary IV line. What happens next? Tennessee officials have not said whether they will try to execute Pike again or explained what went wrong. Her condition could complicate any future attempt. Under Supreme Court precedent, a person can't be executed unless they have a "rational understanding" of why they are being put to death, the New York Times reported . Pike's lawyers have called for her sentence to be commuted. Gov. Lee had denied her clemency before the execution attempt. "I think at the very least the governor should commute Ms. Pike's death sentence to a life sentence," attorney Stephen Ferrell told CNN's State of the Union on Sunday. "We don't know what her physical state will be, but it is clear that she has endured a torturous attempt at executing her." Dr. Zivot said it remains unclear how much pentobarbital entered Pike's system, how much remained in her blood after the injection and what effects she could still experience as she recovers. "I would not, in any way, say at this point that all the big risks are behind her," he said. Professor Russo doubted whether the Supreme Court would stop the state from trying again on double jeopardy grounds — the constitutional protection against being tried or punished twice for the same offense — should it decide to do so. He said, "I think what this Supreme Court would say is, her sentence was to die — to be executed — not to suffer an attempt at execution." "We're in uncharted territory," Robin Maher, executive director of the nonprofit Death Penalty Information Center, told USA Today . "The U.S. Supreme Court has not decided whether a second execution attempt would violate the Constitution since 1947. These are questions that have never needed to be asked before, and no one knows the answers." item.title: Trump looms over Susan Collins and Troy Jackson's first Maine Senate debate
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Susan Collins; Troy Jackson. (Getty) Republican Sen. Susan Collins and Democratic challenger Troy Jackson debated for the first time Tuesday in Maine, trading attacks over President Donald Trump, the cost of living and abortion in one of the most closely watched Senate races in the country . Maine is central to Democrats’ path to the Senate majority as they try to capitalize on Trump’s unpopularity. Jackson tried to do just that Tuesday by tying Collins to Trump, name-checking him at least 20 times in one hour of debating on WGME-TV. “It matters who you stand with,” Jackson said in his opening statement. “I don’t owe Donald Trump and the billionaires anything. I don’t fight for billionaires like she does.” Collins, meanwhile, emphasized multiple instances when she opposed the Trump administration. She also sought to localize the race and pitch her seniority — and her perch as chair of the powerful Senate Appropriations Committee — as a boost to Maine. She touted $1.5 billion in federal funds that she has brought home to the state for 672 projects in the last five years, “from Madawaksa to Kittery, from Eastport to Rumford.” “I’ve been able to bring home federal dollars to help ease the burden on our taxpayers,” Collins said. Jackson set the tone for the debate early by connecting Collins to Trump and repeatedly saying she votes in alignment with him 96% of the time. Collins questioned the methodology of the study he cited. In a moment that captured her tricky relationship with her party’s leader , Collins dodged two questions about whether she would stand with Trump if he visited Maine, with Trump having recently teased a visit to the Pine Tree State. Collins said only that she doesn’t expect him to come and that she’s “not exactly his favorite senator.” Collins’ answer prompted a grin from Jackson. Trump has said Collins is “not my favorite person” but nevertheless endorsed her for re-election, and Vice President JD Vance has gone to Maine and backed her at events . Polls show a neck-and-neck race between Collins and Jackson, often within the margin of error, as Collins seeks to defy gravity yet again and win a sixth term in the blue-leaning state. She is the only GOP senator representing a state Trump lost in 2024. Both parties are spending tens of millions of dollars on a seat that carries major implications for control of the chamber, and a victory for Collins would constrict Democrats’ path to the Senate majority. Jackson also highlighted Collins’ pivotal vote in 2018 to confirm Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh, who was part of the majority that overturned Roe v. Wade, doing away with the federal right to abortion. Tuesday’s debate fell on the anniversary of Kavanaugh’s confirmation vote in the Senate. Collins said she judges all nominees by their qualifications, and she noted that she also supported justices who voted to uphold Roe v. Wade. “In fact, I am the only Republican senator to have voted for Justice [Sonia] Sotomayor, [Elena] Kagan and [Ketanji Brown] Jackson, who were nominated by a Democratic senator,” Collins said. Collins also hit back against attempts to tie her to the end of Roe v. Wade, referring to Jackson’s more conservative stance on abortion earlier in his career and quipping, “There’s only one of us on this stage who has always been pro-choice, and that’s me.” Jackson did not engage with the barb in the moment, but he noted in his closing statement that he pushed for progressive abortion policies in the Legislature. Jackson’s spokesperson, Dan Gottlieb, told NBC News earlier Tuesday that he would oppose any Trump Supreme Court nominee in his final two years should a vacancy open up — a view shared by some other Democrats . Jackson also said Collins voted to advance Trump’s “big, beautiful bill,” which included about $1 trillion in unpopular Medicaid cuts. That sparked a brushback from Collins, who noted that she voted against the legislation when it came to final passage. She said she has “never voted” to cut Medicaid. “He knows I voted against President Trump’s signature legislative accomplishment,” Collins said, adding that she used the process to support a $50 billion rural healthcare fund. Jackson doubled down. “Sen. Collins is like an arsonist who helped set the fire, and she wants credit for bringing a cup of water to put it out,” he said. “She could have stopped it.” Collins went after Jackson’s “failed” policies as a state lawmaker, connecting them to higher housing costs and property taxes. She also questioned his talents as a legislator and whether he could be effective as a junior senator in a divided Senate. When the topic turned to immigration, Jackson cited an ICE officer’s killing of a Mainer this year, saying it happened because “Sen. Collins would not push back against ICE.” Collins said the shooting was “horrific” and “demonstrates that ICE needs further reform.” She said that she supported increased funding for body-worn cameras, as well as training of officers, and that she teamed up with the Maine delegation to demand answers from the Trump administration. In her closing statement, Collins said: “To be effective in the Senate, you need knowledge, experience, seniority and relationships. That combination has allowed me to pass bipartisan legislation.” Jackson questioned whether she has used her power well. “Tonight, Sen. Collins has told us how powerful she is,” he said in his closing statement. “But power means nothing if you won’t use it when the people may need it.” This article was originally published on NBCNews.com This article originally appeared on NBC News at https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2026-election/susan-collins-troy-jackson-clash-trump-seniority-maines-first-senate-d-rcna601346

item.title: Washington resident accused of helping plan Canada's Tumbler Ridge school shooting

People pay their respects at a memorial on the steps of the Town Hall, following a vigil the previous day, in Tumbler Ridge, British Columbia, Canada, Feb. 14, 2026. - Christinne Muschi/The Canadian Press/AP US authorities have arrested a 30-year-old from Washington state in connection with the February school shooting in Tumbler Ridge, British Columbia. James Cody Bryant was arrested in Bellingham, Washington, on Tuesday morning on a charge of conspiracy to murder persons in a foreign country, according to the US Justice Department. The February attack on a secondary school in the small town at the foothills of the Rocky Mountains was Canada’s deadliest school shooting in decades, leaving eight people dead, including six children, and dozens wounded. Bryant appeared in court Tuesday afternoon in Seattle. CNN has reached out to Bryant’s lawyer for comment. A hearing has been set for October 20. Bryant was allegedly “in repeated contact with” the 18-year-old Canadian shooter, Jesse Van Rootselaar, “offering advice, sending money and even agreeing to live stream the horrific event” on Twitch, said Neil Floyd, the acting US attorney for the Western District of Washington, at a press conference in Seattle. The money Bryant gave the shooter amounted to a little over $100, primarily to buy a lighter and a pair of shoes that Van Rootselaar “wanted to have when she conducted this killing spree,” Floyd said. The two discussed sending weapons to Van Rootselaar, but Bryant was uncomfortable with doing so and refused, according to a complaint filed in court on Friday . Bryant began an online friendship with Van Rootselaar after meeting on video chatting website Omegle three years before the shooting, authorities said. An affidavit within the complaint includes excerpts of chat logs between Bryant and Van Rootselaar on the Discord website. “I read a lot of court documents, including some that discuss incredibly heinous acts of violence, but this complaint was particularly difficult to read,” said FBI agent Mike Harrington at the Tuesday press conference, “in part because of the casual tone these two individuals used when discussing the mass taking of innocent lives that was being planned.” In one exchange, Van Rootselaar allegedly told Bryant that she wanted to “avoid doing a school” but that “there’s just so many reasons why it’s ideal.” According to the affidavit, Bryant responded in turn that attacking a hotel “seems like a good idea.” After Van Rootselaar killed two family members, Bryant allegedly offered the attacker advice on how to fix a car when it failed to start en route to the school. Canadian and US authorities have said that Bryant and Van Rootselaar, who died in the shooting, are trans women, though officials used male and female pronouns interchangeably to describe the two throughout the press conference. Assistant Commissioner Elija Rain of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police said Canadian authorities contacted the US Department of Homeland Security soon after the shooting, based on “information from one of the online platforms used by the shooter.” “As further alleged, instead of de-escalating or reporting to law enforcement, Bryant continued to enable the shooter over the months they discussed these plans,” said Harrington. “In addition to providing money, technical advice and particular items to be used in the shooting, Bryant agreed to record a live stream feed of the attack and broadcast it in a way that would maximize notoriety for the shooter.” It was not previously known that anyone apart from Van Rootselaar allegedly participated in planning the massacre. CNN previously reported Van Rootselaar posted about guns and hunting and her apparent mental health struggles online in the lead up to the massacre. Seven families of victims sued tech company OpenAI in April after information emerged that the shooter had used ChatGPT to plan the attack. The week before the suit was filed, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman apologized to the community for not alerting law enforcement after Van Rootselaar’s account was banned. The plan calls for a parcel of the private club to be designated a permanent, official sanctuary for foreign leaders and future U.S. presidents, designed to host international summits and house presidents when they take vacations in Florida, according to a proposal presented to Palm Beach County officials by Trump International Golf Club’s legal counsel. Future presidents would also be offered comped memberships to the Trump club. “Just as Camp David, Windsor Castle, or the Elysee Palace are known worldwide, so too will the Presidential Golf Course in Palm Beach County,” Harvey Oyer, a lawyer representing the Trump course, wrote to the Palm Beach County Board of County Commissioners in a letter last month. Oyer asked the county, which owns the property the course is on, to provide a piece of the land to the federal government, and he promised Trump would pay for the construction of a presidential residence and facilities on that land. Oyer told The Washington Post that a name has yet not been selected for the presidential golf course. “It would further cement Palm Beach County as one of the most recognizable brands and destinations in the world,” Oyer said. A spokesperson for the Trump Organization did not respond to requests for comment. A White House official with knowledge of the proposed plans said in a text message the facilities would provide amenities of a “world-class property.” “The property is minutes away from the Donald J. Trump International Airport, does not have buildings looming, does not have houses along the course, has great security features, is close to law enforcement, and happens to be a highly rated golf course. These are features that are necessary for any presidential retreat,” said the White House official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to preview plans. In the letter, which was first reported by the Palm Beach Post, Oyer said the construction would not be completed before Trump leaves office, so the project would be “a gift” to Trump’s successors and the county would benefit from high-power traffic in the area. The county is seriously considering the proposal and is seeking more information, Palm Beach County Administrator Joseph Abruzzo told The Washington Post. In a meeting last week, Trump representatives assured county officials that, under the proposal, Trump’s company would continue to make lease payments for the golf course and would agree to build the presidential retreat on a connected piece of land that would have a separate entrance from the private club, Abruzzo said. Trump’s club would continue to operate under the Trump family company and would probably benefit from more business if it becomes a site of long-lasting presidential importance. The county is in contact with the General Services Administration, the agency that manages federal properties, and the county will be selecting a parcel of the land for the proposal, Abruzzo said. “My understanding is that President Trump views this as a lasting contribution to the presidency and to those who will hold the office after him,” Abruzzo said. Though presidents already have a retreat at Camp David, Trump has visited the complex less frequently than many of his predecessors, preferring to spend his weekends and holidays at his own properties. He once commented that Camp David’s rustic charm would wear off after half an hour. Previous presidents have left their own marks on the woodsy Maryland retreat. Franklin D. Roosevelt established the getaway for federal workers as a presidential compound and dubbed it Shangri-La, though Dwight D. Eisenhower later named it after his father and grandson. Marjorie Merriweather Post, who was once the wealthiest woman in the United States, also had hoped to create a presidential retreat in the South. She gifted her Palm Beach estate - better known as Mar-a-Lago - to the federal government upon her death in 1973, with the intention that it be turned into a Winter White House. But the National Park Service returned the property to her estate due to high maintenance costs, and Trump bought the property in 1985. Trump International Golf Club opened in 1999 after Trump settled a lawsuit with the county regarding airplanes flying over Mar-a-Lago and the county agreed to lend him the land. Near the golf course, state officials have branded the Palm Beach airport and the road along it with Trump’s name. Trump’s influence over Palm Beach and its image would be further cemented if the golf club becomes a presidential retreat. The wealthy strip of South Florida has undergone a MAGA transformation with Trump’s base flocking to Mar-a-Lago for political events and networking. The nearby golf club has become a go-to destination for Trump spotting. Trump reported an income of nearly $37 million last year from the golf course in his latest financial disclosure. Although Trump had mocked former president Barack Obama for golfing during his presidency, Trump has frequently golfed since he has been in office. One online tracker calculated that Trump has spent at least 137 days in his second term golfing. Rick Reilly, a former Sports Illustrated columnist who wrote “Commander in Cheat: How Golf Explains Trump,” has golfed with Trump and said the president is less interested in the sport than the attention he gains at his own clubs. Reilly described how Trump always plays first in his golfing party and speeds on his golf cart to the next hole, wrapping up his game in less time than is typical, before heading to the clubhouse, where he makes the rounds, talking to his members and fans. If the Palm Beach club were a destination for foreign leaders, they would be part of the display of influence. “I suppose he wants to make a power play with these people and show them who is the king of America,” Reilly said. Don Van Natta Jr., an ESPN senior writer who wrote “First Off the Tee: Presidential Hackers, Duffers, and Cheaters From Taft to Bush,” a book on the history of presidents who golfed, said 17 of the past 20 presidents have golfed. The first avid golfer in the Oval Office was William Howard Taft, and the last president who didn’t golf was Jimmy Carter. “There is a long history of presidents playing golf,” Van Natta said. “It’s an escape where they can, as President [Bill] Clinton told me for my book, to be out in nature, and it’s an escape hatch from the pressures of the Oval Office.” CORRECTION: A photo caption with a previous version of this article and on the homepage omitted the year that President Donald Trump arrived at Trump International Golf Club to watch the Super Bowl. item.title: Russia hits Ukraine with drones and missiles, killing at least 15 people
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Olena Harmash and Vladyslav Smilianets KYIV, Oct 7 (Reuters) - Russia pounded Ukraine with waves of missiles and drones in one of its most "vile strikes" on Wednesday, President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said, killing at least 20 people, including children, and damaging industrial facilities and energy infrastructure. Zelenskiy said the strike coincided with Russian ‌President Vladimir Putin's birthday. The heaviest death toll was in Pryluky in the northern Chernihiv region, where a Russian missile obliterated a five-storey residential building. At least ‌14 people, including four children, were killed there, local officials said. "Today, as a birthday 'gift' to Putin, the Russian army destroyed a residential building in Pryluky...," Zelenskiy said. "The Russians wanted to strike painfully and demonstratively. This was one ​of the most vile strikes: 70 missiles in total, many of them ballistic." An excavator and dozens of rescuers with shovels sifted through rubble at the site where several sections of the five-storey building collapsed. Emergency workers used ladders to get to the upper floors of what remained of the building. Around 50 people were wounded, including seven children, regional officials said. BIG JUMP IN REPORTED DRONE INTERCEPTIONS Zelenskiy said six other people were killed in Kyiv, Oleksandria and Kremenchuk during the heavy overnight attack. Russia's defence ministry said its forces had carried out a "massive strike" on military-industrial facilities ‌in Kyiv and other Ukrainian regions, using high-precision land-, sea- and ⁠air-launched weapons, as well as drones. Ukraine's air force said it had downed just over 80% of the 46 jet-powered drones launched by Russia — a sharp increase from recent weeks when, on average, air defences took down 50% to 60%. Since the summer, Russia has used increasing numbers ⁠of the new high-velocity drones in round-the-clock attacks on Kyiv and other cities, with Ukraine's air defences struggling to cope with their speed. The air force did not explain the jump in the interception rate and did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Zelenskiy said the Russian ballistic missiles remained the major challenge for Ukraine, adding that he and his team were "every day looking for Patriot (missile interception) ​systems ​that can and must protect people's lives". Ukraine received a new €1.2 billion ($1.34 billion) tranche from the European Union ​on Wednesday and will channel the funds towards defence needs, Prime Minister ‌Sergii Koretskyi said. The US-made Patriot system is the only weapon in Ukraine's arsenal capable of stopping high-velocity ballistic missiles but tight global supplies have been drained by the Iran war as well as the Ukraine conflict. Ukraine's energy ministry said it had started to roll out partial emergency power cuts in five Ukrainian regions due to the attacks. Russia's defence ministry said its targets included sites where Ukrainian defence company Fire Point manufactures and stores its Flamingo cruise missiles and medium- and long-range drones in Kyiv as well as regions of Kyiv, Chernihiv, Kirovohrad, Dnipropetrovsk, Poltava and Kharkiv. Last week Zelenskiy said Ukraine had fired its first domestically made ballistic missile in combat, produced by Fire Point. In an interview with Reuters, he ‌said he expected the company to have a longer-range FP-9 missile ready by the autumn. Fire Point ​has said that weapon will be able to reach Moscow. PEOPLE SHELTER OVERNIGHT IN KYIV METRO Zelenskiy said Ukrainian troops ​hit four targets in Russia over the past 24 hours, including two Russian ​oil facilities and a training ground in the Perm, Samara, and Astrakhan regions. In the Reuters interview, Zelenskiy said Ukraine would hit Russia's energy ‌assets in response to Moscow's escalating strikes on civilian infrastructure. Many Kyiv residents ​took shelter in the city's deep underground metro ​stations as warnings of the upcoming attacks were shared by Ukrainian officials and military intelligence. Several loud explosions reverberated through the capital during the night. "The metro is better because we live on the 9th floor of a high-rise, and it's really scary when you're on the 9th floor and missiles are flying at you," Lesia, ​a 49-year-old Kyiv resident, told Reuters. Ukrainian officials said Russian ballistic missiles ‌as well as the drones had targeted Kyiv. Overnight air strikes on the southeastern city of Dnipro damaged an industrial facility, transport infrastructure in Zaporizhzhia and ​apartment buildings in Kremenchuk, regional officials said on the Telegram messaging app. ($1 = 0.8947 euros) (Reporting by Olena Harmash in Kyiv and Vladislav Smilianets in Pryluky, additional ​reporting by Yuliia Dysa, Jekaterīna Golubkova; Editing by Daniel Flynn, Andrew Heavens and Gareth Jones) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://uk.news.yahoo.com/russia-strikes-ukraines-kyiv-fresh-014448221.html

item.title: More than 20 million people are getting a $90 Social Security check, while 40 million aren't
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Millions of Medicare beneficiaries will receive a $90 payment from the Social Security Administration this week as part of an effort to lower health care costs for older Americans. President Trump announced on Oct. 2 that the administration would send a one-time payment to around one-third of people enrolled in Medicare Part B, which covers doctors' visits, outpatient care and preventive screenings. In a White House statement, the Trump administration said the "premium rebates" were intended to help "enrollees pay for their Medicare Part B premiums." The payments will be issued automatically to 20.8 million qualified Medicare beneficiaries starting this week. Most enrollees will receive a direct deposit for $90 on or around Oct. 8. Paper checks will be sent to some beneficiaries later this month. The rebate comes from the Medicare Improvement Fund, which was set up by Congress in 2008 to make improvements to Medicare Parts A and B. The $90 payment will cover less than half of the standard monthly Part B premium, which is $202.90 for 2026, up from $185 in 2025. Some have warned that the payments do not go far enough to cover increasing Medicare expenses. Juliette Cubanski, director of Medicare policy at KFF, a nonprofit health policy organization, said Part B annual premiums are expected to rise by $79 in 2027, which would consume "most of the $90 payment." The KFF added that the Medicare Improvement Fund would be drained by the measure. Who gets the payment, and who doesn't? The payments will be sent to 20.8 million Americans who are covered by original Medicare Part B, according to a fact sheet released by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS). To qualify, beneficiaries must: Be living in the U.S. Not receive premium assistance from Medicaid, and Are not higher earners who pay a surcharge on top of the standard premium. Beneficiaries enrolled in Medicare Advantage are also not eligible. Around 40 million Part B enrollees, or roughly two-thirds of the total, will not receive the payment. The biggest group left out is the 35.2 million people on Medicare Advantage, the private-plan alternative to traditional Medicare. Those eligible for the payment will receive the rebate via direct deposit from the Social Security Administration, CMS says. Those without direct deposit will receive a check at the mailing address Medicare has on file. Those who think they qualify for the payments but are unsure can call 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227) to check their eligibility for the premium rebate, according to CMS guidance . Beneficiaries who want to check the status of their payment should call the Social Security Administration at 1-800-772-1213 starting Oct. 15. item.title: Fuel industry warns truck stops not to sell red dye diesel after Trump lifts restrictions
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Truck stops nationwide were warned to “proceed with caution” Tuesday by a major industry group after President Donald Trump signed an executive order to promote the use of “red dye” diesel fuel. Red dye diesel is exempt from federal excise taxes because it is intended for farm equipment and other off-road uses. The order, signed before farmers in Nebraska on Monday night, aims to bring down fuel prices by “temporarily” allowing highway use of red dye diesel fuel, according to a White House statement . U.S. voters are deeply frustrated by the high price of gas, and the Trump administration is under intense pressure to bring down fuel costs before the Nov. 3 midterm elections. Monday’s order instructs Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to “defer certain diesel fuel tax payment obligations and to provide penalty relief to the extent permitted by law.” It does not waive the federal taxes, because only Congress can eliminate a tax. Following Trump’s directive, the Energy Marketers of America warned gas stations to “proceed with caution.” “Whether relief is available, whom it covers, and on what conditions depend on Treasury determinations and guidance not yet issued,” the group said. “Deferral is not forgiveness.” Moreover, the order does not “resolve EPA or state restrictions” on the dyed variety of diesel fuel, the EMA said. A White House official emphasized that federal agencies have wide discretion over enforcement actions, telling NBC News that the IRS would announce its determination soon as to whether it will enforce the deferred diesel tax. But other trucking and gas industry groups sounded a note of caution similar to the EMA’s. “The White House appears to be trying to encourage the supply chain to move toward selling dyed fuel in non-traditional ways,” the Society of Independent Gasoline Marketers of America and the National Association of Truck Stop Owners said in a note to their members. “We do not expect most reputable diesel retailers and fuel marketers to do this,” they said. “First, the tax is still owed, so there’s limited upside.” In addition, “the logistical challenges outweigh any visible upside: Residual dye lingers in tanks and fuel systems.” For most fuel sellers, “the liability and customer risk outweigh any temporary, uncertain benefit.” White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers disputed that characterization of the executive order. “President Trump’s executive action will quickly cut diesel costs and put money directly back into the pockets of American truckers, saving them over $100 every time they refill at the gas pump,” she told NBC News. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, she said, will “coordinate with states, industry leadership, and labor organizations to ensure access to dyed diesel.” Despite an executive order promoting red dye diesel, trucking and fuel industry groups are warning their members it may not be worth the risk. (Clayton Steward / Bloomberg via Getty) A group representing independent long-haul truckers also suggested Trump’s move would provide little benefit to its members. “Allowing the wider use of red-dyed diesel will provide minimal relief. Market stability is essential to bring down costs for the long haul,” said Todd Spencer, president of the Owner-Operator Independent Drivers Association. Since the war with Iran began, the price of diesel has surged from $3.76 per gallon to $6.32 as of Tuesday, a nearly 70% increase. The Iran conflict is not the only conflict contributing to diesel’s skyrocketing price. A recent escalation of the Ukraine-Russia war has included strikes by Ukrainian drones on Russian refineries. Russia, traditionally one of the world’s large diesel exporters, has responded to the attacks by imposing a diesel export ban through at least the end of October. Trump has urged Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to halt strikes on Russia’s diesel infrastructure . “Mr. Zelenskyy has to do one thing. He has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia,” Trump told reporters in early September . “There are plenty of other targets. Don’t hit diesel fuel, because that’s hurting the world.” Oil prices also remain sharply elevated since the beginning of the year. Brent crude oil, which traded Tuesday night above $101 per barrel, is up more than 66% since the start of the year. Congress has already taken action to eliminate the lowest rung — the penny — and now another coin collecting dust in people's wallets could be on the chopping block next. The House and Senate both passed bills earlier this year aimed at eliminating the penny once and for all. The bipartisan Common Cents Act was unanimously approved in each chamber, but has yet to get President Donald Trump's signature to become law. It followed the Treasury Department announcing last December that the U.S. Mint would no longer produce pennies, which at the time cost more than three times their value to make. item.description:

Health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor says no special measures have been ordered regarding a reported plague death in Russia (Igor IVANKO) The United States made a formal request pressing Russia for information on the reported plague death of a laboratory technician, a source close to the matter said Tuesday, as calls grew for transparency from Moscow. Russian authorities have denied that they are imposing anti-plague measures and played down the reports of an incident at a plague research institute in Siberia's Irkutsk region last week. But US President Donald Trump said he would speak soon with Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin, while US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and the World Health Organization's head called on Moscow to be open about the situation. "We have officially requested additional information from the Russian government," a State Department spokesperson said Tuesday. "We are also in official communication with other countries around the world to share information," they added. The request for information was sent via a confidential diplomatic communication, known as a demarche, according to a source close to the matter. During a trip to Iceland, Rubio said: "We encourage Russia to be transparent and share more information with the world so that all of us could react accordingly and appropriately." Trump later said he would be speaking to Putin about what happened. "I have a call scheduled, yes," Trump told reporters at the White House when asked if he had spoken to Putin, adding that it would happen "very soon." Asked what US intelligence agencies were saying about the situation, Trump said: "We're in very deep discussions. We'll be able to report on it probably tomorrow." - Cause of death 'undetermined' - Russian news outlet People of Baikal reported Friday that the dead woman -- named as 28-year-old Darya Shipilova -- may have contracted pneumonic plague from a broken test tube. Other media reported a possible link between her death and a lab accident at the facility. item.description:

Nidal Hasan, who was sentenced to death for the 2009 mass shooting at Fort Hood, Texas, will be executed by firing squad on Dec. 3, according to a memo from the acting Army secretary. The execution, the first carried out by the U.S. military in more than 60 years, is scheduled for 1 p.m. CT, according to the memo issued Tuesday by acting Army Secretary Adam Telle. The Pentagon announced Monday that Hasan would be executed by firing squad after President Donald Trump approved the decision Friday. Handout/Getty Images - PHOTO: Maj. Nidal Hasan Moved To Jail Under the military’s execution process for prisoners on death row, the Army secretary initiates the proceedings, which then require approval from the defense secretary and eventually the president. Under Army policy, executions must happen within 150 days of the president approving it, but no sooner than 60 days. The military has not executed a service member since 1961, when Pvt. John Bennett was put to death after being convicted of the rape and attempted murder of an 11-year-old girl in Austria. On Nov. 5, 2009, Hasan, then an Army psychiatrist, opened fire at the Soldier Readiness Processing Center at the Fort Hood military base, killing 12 soldiers and one civilian before he was shot, severely wounded and arrested. Hasan was convicted of 13 counts of premeditated murder and 32 counts of attempted murder and sentenced to death in 2013. He was sent to a military detention center at Fort Leavenworth in Kansas. He is one of four death row inmates in the Army justice system. The announcement of his execution comes after ABC News reported in June that the Army had been planning military executions , according to internal documents and officials familiar with the matter. Army regulation dictates that at least two media outlets should be selected to witness the execution.
